books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.text: Paraphrase, from the grounding books, of the two rival plans for readmitting the Southern states. Lincoln’s Ten Percent Plan (1863): when 10 percent of a state’s 1860 voters swore an oath of allegiance to the Union and accepted emancipation, the state could form a new government and send representatives to Congress. The Wade-Davis Bill (1864): a state could return only after a majority of its voters swore an “ironclad” oath of past and present loyalty, and its new constitution had to abolish slavery. The bill also extended the laws for white persons to all persons. Lincoln pocket-vetoed the bill.
stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of Lincoln’s Ten Percent Plan and the Wade-Davis Bill, from Barron’s Premium 2027, Chapter 7, and 5 Steps to a 5, 2024, Chapter 16. No wording is quoted from either plan.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: A student claims the Wade-Davis Bill was written to give Black men the vote. The best response is that

options.text: the bill did give Black men the vote in every Southern state at once.
options.misconception: Background: the bill required a majority oath and extended the laws for white persons to all persons, but it made no provision for Black suffrage.

options.text: Lincoln’s plan, not Wade-Davis, gave Black men the vote.
options.misconception: Background: Lincoln’s plan said nothing about Black suffrage either.

options.text: neither plan gave Black men the vote; the Reconstruction Acts and the Fifteenth Amendment did.
the bill gave the vote only to Black women.
options.misconception: Background: no Reconstruction plan gave the vote to women.

rationales.A: Background: the bill required a majority oath and extended the laws for white persons to all persons, but it made no provision for Black suffrage.
rationales.B: Background: Lincoln’s plan said nothing about Black suffrage either.
rationales.C: Neither Lincoln’s plan nor Wade-Davis gave Black men the vote. The vote came two years later, when the Reconstruction Acts required Black suffrage in new state constitutions, and the Fifteenth Amendment wrote it into the Constitution in 1870.
rationales.D: Background: no Reconstruction plan gave the vote to women.
rationales.general:
1. Read what each plan actually requires: oaths, loyalty, and trial laws extended to all persons.
2. Neither one mentions Black suffrage.
3. Background: the vote arrived later, through the Reconstruction Acts and the Fifteenth Amendment.
4. So the claim gives Wade-Davis a victory that belongs to later laws.
Remember: when a claim names the wrong law, ask which later law did the job.
